Back when automobiles first became numerous, it was decided that some kind of a signaling system should be devised to keep them from colliding with each other at street intersections. What wound up working best was the same system that had long been used by ships at sea. Ships used red lights on their port sides, green lights on their starboard sides, and white lights on their sterns, and also displayed white lights when at anchor. In a situation where one ship had to cross in front of another, the protocol was and is that if your ship is crossing at night in front of a ship that is approaching from your port or left side, you will see that ships green starboard running light. Green means go, therefore you are the stand on vessel and your obligation is to maintain your course and speed. The other vessel will be seeing your red port running light as you approach from her starboard or right side. Red means stop, so this vessel is the give way vessel, and is obligated to take whatever means are neccesary to stay out of the way of your stand on vessel. Most often, this means simply changing course or speed, but in a close quarters situation can mean stopping altogether, or even backing down. Any vessel seeing a white light ahead at night must assume that they are either overtaking another vessel or approaching one that is anchored. Both overtaken and anchored vessels are privileged under the rules of the nautical road. The overtaking vessel or approaching vessel is required to stay out of their way to avoid collision. From the white light came the yellow traffic light, probably yellow to avoid confusion with the many other lights you might see along a street in the city. The same rules apply day or night to vessels at sea. In daylight, the lights may not be visible but port, starboard, or astern can be visually determined.
 If you are in a collision at sea, hitting another vessel on her port, or red light, side is very much like running a red light and colliding with another vehicle. Quite likely, you will be looked upon as the guilty party. On the other hand, if you hit another vessel on her starboard, or green light, side you have still been in a collision, which isn't good, but it is more like you were proceeding through an intersection on a green light and someone ran a red light and you hit them. There isn't an automatic presumption that you are guilty as there might be if you had run a red light. Colliding with a vessel from astern when overtaking, or with an anchored vessel is like rear-ending another car or hitting a parked car. 
 Admiralty law almost always apportions blame between colliding vessels. Collisions at sea are frowned upon, and every mariner has the obligation to avoid them, so when one occurs there is usually enough blame that everyone involved gets to share in it. If you have to be in a collision between vessels, the least undesirable kind would be the one where your anchored vessel is hit by another ship. Next least would be to have the other ship hit you on the stern while it is overtaking you, followed by having another ship hit you on your red light side. The very least desirable collision to be in is when another vessel hits you on your green light side. No matter the circumstances, the appearance of this kind of collision is that you were attempting to run a red light and got hit. Unfortunately, that is the situation the "Fitzgerald" is in. No matter if the merchant vessel reversed course a half hour before, it is still highly inadvisable to attempt to pass in front of them when you are the give way vessel.
